analysis.one_liner: Replaces all federal income and payroll taxes with a 23% national sales tax and shuts down the IRS.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2013 and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal income tax, payroll taxes, and the estate tax, and replace them with a national 23% sales tax on goods and services. Every family would get a monthly rebate covering the tax on poverty-level spending. States that already run sales taxes would collect the federal tax for a fee, and the IRS would be phased out. The new tax would automatically end if the constitutional amendment authorizing the income tax were not repealed within seven years.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most: their income, capital gains, and investment income would no longer be taxed at all, and the estate tax on inherited wealth would disappear. Purchases made for business or investment purposes are explicitly exempt, so wealth built through buying assets would go untaxed [S2][S3]. All taxpayers would stop filing income tax returns [S2]. Lower-income families would get a monthly rebate covering sales tax on poverty-level purchases [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and wealthy estates

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the income tax, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift taxes, ending income tax filing for every household [S2][S3].
Exempts purchases made for business, export, or investment purposes from the sales tax, so asset purchases are never taxed [S2][S3].
Provides a monthly rebate to every registered family equal to the sales tax on the federal poverty level for the family's size, so no one pays the tax on basic subsistence spending [S2][S3].
Shifts collection to state tax agencies, which keep a fee of one-quarter of one percent of collections, and pays registered sellers an administration credit for the cost of collecting [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who buys goods and services, since the 23% tax applies to nearly all consumption. Lower- and middle-income households spend most of what they earn, so they pay the tax on essentially their whole income; the rebate offsets only poverty-level spending. Very high earners, who save and invest much of their income, would pay tax on a small share of theirs. Social Security and Medicare funding would shift from dedicated payroll taxes to general sales tax revenue.

drawbacks.text: A consumption tax falls hardest on households that spend most of their income; the rebate only offsets the tax up to the poverty level, so a working family earning above poverty pays the 23% rate on everything it buys beyond that [S2][S3].
The rebate is not automatic: families must register annually, certify lawful residency for each member, and list Social Security numbers, or they stop receiving payments [S3].
The 23% rate is stated on a tax-inclusive basis (about 30 cents per dollar of pre-tax price) and would come on top of existing state sales taxes, a large jump in the tax on everyday purchases [S3].

Repealing payroll taxes while redirecting general sales tax revenue into the Social Security and Medicare trust funds makes their funding depend entirely on future consumption tax collections and annual rate adjustments [S2].
The new sales tax would terminate after seven years unless the Sixteenth Amendment is repealed, leaving the tax system on an unstable footing if the constitutional repeal fails [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ending income tax filing and payroll withholding would be a real simplification, and the rebate protects the poorest households. But the core trade is replacing a tax graded by income with a tax graded by spending: families that must spend what they earn pay the full rate on most of it, while the largest untaxed income — capital gains, inheritances, investment returns — belongs to the wealthiest households, and business and investment purchases are exempt by design. Weighing the bill honestly, the distribution of the tax burden moves markedly toward ordinary working households and away from concentrated wealth, layered on top of a higher visible tax on daily purchases.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Chambliss introduced the Fair Tax Act of 2013 with seven original cosponsors on January 23, 2013 [S5][S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
Eight senators, all Republicans, cosponsored the bill; it drew no Democratic support [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained or lost money; the existing income tax system and its progressive structure simply remained in place, which is the outcome opponents of the bill preferred.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; the current tax system stayed

for.name: Saxby Chambliss
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S1][S5].

for.name: 8 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Senators Burr, Inhofe, Coburn, Cornyn, Moran, and Cruz [S4][S3].

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing or markup was ever held [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; the bill never advanced past the Democratic-chaired Finance Committee [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill eliminates the income tax on wages, capital gains, and investment returns and repeals the estate tax, while purchases made for investment purposes are exempt. The tax burden shifts to consumption, which is a larger share of income for working families.

industries.industry: Retailers and sellers of goods and services
industries.note: Sellers would become collectors of a 23% federal sales tax, taking on new registration, reporting, and bonding duties, but the bill pays them an administration credit of at least $200 or 0.25% of tax remitted to cover the cost.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax advisory industry
industries.note: Repealing the income tax and defunding the IRS after 2017 would eliminate most income tax filing and compliance work, the industry's core market.
States with existing sales taxes would become the permanent collection channel for the federal sales tax and would keep a 0.25% administration fee, embedding them in federal tax administration.
